2 Dynamic Packet Filter                                                      2.1 DPF/Operating system interface
DPF’s packet filter language is a declarative language that is used by            The DPF system is modular and easily integrated into network
protocols to describe the message headers that they are looking for.         subsystems. Its public interface (given in Table 1) is comprised
Similarly to the languages used in MPF [27] and PATHFINDER [1],              of three functions: dpf insert (used to insert a filter), dpf demux
it can handle a wide range of possible protocols and supports frag-          (used to demultiplex messages), and dpf delete (used to delete
mentation.                                                                   filters). System specific details of message alignment, minimum
     A DPF packet filter is composed of a sequence of boolean com-           packet size, cache flushing, and a memory allocation function are
parisons (or atoms) linked by conjunctions. Logically, a filter’s            provided as defaults that can be overridden.
atoms are checked in order after packet reception (our declarative
language avoids most side-effects, allowing re-ordering for effi-            3 Implementation
ciency). If all atoms are true, then the filter accepts and the packet
is delivered to the associated application.                                  This section first discusses how DPF uses dynamic code generation
     Figure 1 shows an example packet filter. Each atom is specified         and then reports on a number of optimizations that it performs.
using the standard set of arithmetic operators, with the addition of
the ‘:’ and SHIFT operators. The ‘:’ operator is used to read packet         3.1 Dynamic code generation
data. It takes as arguments a base (specified in bytes) and a size
(specified in bits). The base can be either a constant or an indirect        DPF exploits dynamic code generation in two ways: by using it to
load from the message itself. The SHIFT operation shifts the base of         eliminate interpretation overhead by compiling packet filters into
the message pointer, allowing arbitrary predicates to be composed            executable code, and by using filter constants to aggressively opti-
using relative addressing.                                                   mize this executable code. For portability, DPF uses the machine-
     A new filter is merged into the set of active filters as follows:       independent VCODE dynamic code generation system [8].

                                                                         2
        Operation                                                             Description
        int dpf insert(struct dpf ir *filter)                                 dpf insert inserts filter filter. It fails if the filter is malformed, if
                                                                              memory allocation required to incorporate it fails, or, optionally, if
                                                                              the filter is already present. On success it returns a filter id.
        int dpf delete(int fid)                                               Delete filter fid inserted using dpf insert. It fails if the filter does
                                                                              not exist.
        int (*dpf demux)(void *msg, unsigned nbytes)                          The function pointer dpf demux is called to demultiplex a packet.
                                                                              It takes as arguments a pointer to the message (msg) and a message
                                                                              size, in bytes (nbytes). It returns the id of the accepting filter, or “0”
                                                                              if no filter accepts.

in isolating the effects of dynamic code generation. To this end,               Atom coalescing The first optimization in this category is the co-

Alignment estimation Because neither packet filters nor mes-                         # Check Ethernet header
sages can be trusted, traditional packet-filter systems perform a                    # (12:16  ==   0x8) &&
number of checks to guard against errors. For example, packet-filter                 lhu     t1, 12(a0)    # 12:16 (a0 holds pointer to message)
engines treat every load and store as potentially unaligned. Mem-                    li      t0, 0x8       # Load 0x8
                                                                                     bne     t1,t0,$next   # Branch to next filter if not equal
ory operations must therefore first be checked for proper alignment
to eliminate unaligned access traps. We optimize this process by                     # SHIFT(6   + 6 + 2) && (is optimized away)
finding a lower bound for the alignment of the message-pointer
base register. The general algorithm is to record the effects of every               # Check protocol: TCP is 6
SHIFT instruction on the base message register. For example, this                    # (9:8 ==   6) &&
register starts word-aligned: if all subsequent shifts are by constants              lbu         +
                                                                                            t1,9 14(a0)     # 9:8 after propogating ethernet header size
that are multiples of four, then this bound stays the same. However,                 li     t0,6            # load 6
if a shift by two bytes occurs, then the lower bound on this register                bne    t1,t0,$next     # Branch to next filter if not equal
becomes two.
     As a side-effect of alignment information propagation DPF                 Figure 2: Generated MIPS R3000 code to recognize the first three
eliminates constant SHIFT operations by adding its operand to the              atoms of an Ethernet/IP/TCP header (after optimization).
message offset of subsequent atoms. This optimization saves about
one addition instruction for each protocol header.

     The performance of the user-level implementations of UDP
and TCP using DPF are as good as hard-coded in-kernel imple-                  We have presented a packet filter system, DPF, that uses dynamic
mentations and better than other user-level implementations of the            code generation to improve the performance of its packet-classifier
internet protocols in user space over Ethernet [25, 15]. In fact,             engine by 13–26 times that of the best numbers presented in the liter-
our user-level implementations perform close to the possible limits;          ature. Since the code DPF generates can exploit filter constants that
Thekkath and Levy measure 340 microseconds between 25-MHz                     are not available to static implementations, it can even be faster than
DECstation 5000/200s for a user-level reliable raw RPC proto-                 hand-crafted demultiplexing routines. Its performance shows that
col [22], while we are measuring 309 microseconds on a faster                 packet filters can work well even in the context of Gb/sec networks;
machine (40-MHz) but using IP and UDP with checksumming.
